A lizard is a type of reptile — a scaly, cold-blooded animal. It is one of the largest groups of reptiles on Earth, with over 6,000 known species.

Think of a lizard as the "classic reptile" most people picture in their minds. Here are the key features that define one:

Body shape: Most lizards have a long, slender body with four legs, a long tail, and a distinct head. Their entire body is covered in scales, which can be smooth, rough, or even spiky depending on the species.

Eyelids and ears: Unlike snakes (which are their close relatives), most lizards have movable eyelids — meaning they can blink — and visible ear openings on the sides of their head. These two features are one of the clearest ways to tell a lizard apart from a snake.

Cold-blooded: Lizards are ectothermic, which means they cannot generate their own body heat. They depend entirely on the sun and their surroundings to warm up. This is why you often see lizards sitting motionless in the sun — they are literally charging themselves with warmth before they can become active.

Tongue: Many lizards flick their forked or pointed tongue in and out constantly. They use it to "taste" the air and detect smells — it is essentially their nose.

Lizards vary dramatically in size. On one end, you have geckos that are just a few centimetres long and weigh almost nothing. On the other end, the Komodo dragon — the world's largest lizard — can grow up to 3 metres (about 10 feet) long and weigh over 70 kilograms (150 pounds). It is a powerful predator capable of killing deer and pigs.

Lizards are found almost everywhere on Earth — on every continent except Antarctica. They thrive in:

  • Deserts (like the thorny devil in Australia)
  • Tropical rainforests (like chameleons in Africa)
  • Grasslands and open fields
  • Rocky mountains
  • Backyards and city walls (like the common house gecko)

They are especially diverse and abundant in warm, sunny regions because they need external heat to survive.

Most lizards are carnivores or insectivores — they eat insects, worms, small mammals, birds, or even other lizards. Some, like the iguana, are herbivores that eat leaves, flowers, and fruit. A few are omnivores and eat both plants and animals.

Tail-dropping: Many lizards have a remarkable defence trick called autotomy — the ability to voluntarily detach their own tail when grabbed by a predator. The detached tail wriggles on the ground to distract the attacker, while the lizard escapes. A new tail eventually grows back, though it is often made of cartilage rather than bone and looks slightly different.

Camouflage: Some lizards, most famously chameleons, can change their skin colour. This is used for communication, temperature regulation, and sometimes camouflage.

Running on water: The basilisk lizard can sprint across the surface of water on its hind legs for short distances — earning it the nickname "the Jesus Christ lizard."

Venomous species: A small number of lizards are venomous. The Gila monster and the Mexican beaded lizard are the most well-known venomous lizards. The Komodo dragon also has venom in addition to bacteria-laden saliva.

Reproduction: Most lizards lay eggs, but some species give birth to live young. A few can even reproduce without mating, through a process called parthenogenesis.

No — but they are close relatives. Snakes evolved from lizard-like ancestors and are classified in the same broad group (Squamata). The key differences: snakes have no legs, no eyelids (their eyes are always open, covered by a transparent scale), and no external ear openings. Some lizards, however, are also legless (like the glass lizard), which can cause confusion — but even legless lizards still have eyelids and ear openings, which snakes do not.
How "Lizard" is Used in Everyday Language

Beyond the literal animal, the word "lizard" appears in a few informal and figurative expressions:

  • "Lounge lizard" — an old-fashioned, slightly mocking term for a man who hangs around bars, parties, or social events, often trying to charm or impress people in a slimy or insincere way. The image is of someone lazy and cold-blooded, like a lizard lounging in the sun.
  • "Lizard brain" — an informal phrase used to refer to the most primitive, instinct-driven part of human thinking (survival instincts, fear, aggression). The idea comes from the fact that reptiles have a simpler brain structure compared to mammals, focused on basic survival.
  • In conspiracy culture, "lizard" or "lizard people" is sometimes used mockingly or seriously to refer to the idea that powerful figures are secretly reptilian — this is generally treated as a fringe conspiracy theory.

A lizard is a scaly, four-legged (usually), cold-blooded reptile with eyelids and ear openings, found across the globe in thousands of forms — from tiny backyard geckos to enormous Komodo dragons. They are sun-dependent, often insect-eating animals known for their adaptability, their flickering tongues, and their remarkable ability to drop and regrow their tails.
